title: Where the speed went
intro: Hardware got roughly a thousand times faster and a million times roomier. Opening a program still takes about a second, booting still takes about half a minute, and a computer still occasionally makes you wait. Software expanded to fill the space almost exactly as fast as the space appeared, and the reasons for that are not all bad ones.

blocks.title: Nothing gets faster for long
blocks.text: In 1995 a rule of thumb circulated that what Intel gives, Microsoft takes away. It was a joke about Windows, but the pattern is general and it is not really about laziness. Every generation of hardware allows something that was previously impossible, developers build that thing, and the machine ends up as busy as it ever was doing work the old machine could not have attempted.

blocks.name: MS-DOS 1.0
blocks.spec: 12 KB of memory, one 160 KB floppy, boots in seconds
blocks.text: The operating system fitted on a floppy disk with room to spare for your program. It also did essentially nothing: no windows, no multitasking, no networking, no protection between programs, and no drivers for hardware it did not already know about.

blocks.name: Windows 3.0
blocks.spec: 384 KB minimum, 640 KB recommended, 6 MB disk
blocks.text: Overlapping windows, a mouse, and several programs on screen at once. The memory requirement is roughly forty times DOS, for capabilities the earlier system did not attempt.

blocks.name: Windows 95
blocks.spec: 4 MB minimum, 8 MB realistic, 40 to 55 MB disk
blocks.text: Ran acceptably on 8 MB and well on 16. The joke at the time was that the recommended specification was always the machine you were about to buy, not the one you owned, and it was mostly true.

blocks.name: Windows XP
blocks.spec: 64 MB minimum, 128 MB realistic, 1.5 GB disk
blocks.text: Thirty times the disk footprint of Windows 95, six years later. It also brought proper memory protection, so one crashing program stopped taking the machine down with it, which is worth several hundred megabytes on its own.

blocks.name: Windows Vista
blocks.spec: 512 MB minimum, 1 GB realistic, 15 GB disk
blocks.text: The clearest case of software outrunning the hardware people actually owned. Machines were sold as Vista Capable that could not run it comfortably, and the resulting reputation took years to shake off. A useful lesson in what a minimum specification really means.

blocks.name: Windows 10
blocks.text: The requirement stopped climbing steeply, partly because processors stopped getting dramatically faster and partly because tablets and cheap laptops set a floor that software had to respect.

blocks.name: Windows 11
blocks.text: The disk figure grew more than the memory figure, and the hard requirement is not performance at all but a security chip, which made a large number of perfectly capable machines ineligible.

blocks.title: Games, where the demand always shows up first
blocks.text: Games are the software that has always asked for everything available and then some. Install sizes are the clearest single measure, because they track texture resolution, audio quality and the sheer amount of content, all of which grew with what storage and memory allowed.

blocks.name: Doom
blocks.text: The whole game fitted on eight floppy disks. It was distributed as shareware, meaning the first episode was given away free, which is part of why almost every PC of the era had it.

blocks.name: Half-Life
blocks.text: One CD. Thirty times Doom in five years, mostly texture and audio data.

blocks.name: Half-Life 2
blocks.spec: 4.5 GB, 256 MB RAM, five CDs or one DVD
blocks.text: Ten times again in six years. This is also the game that introduced a great many people to the idea that software would be delivered over the internet and would check in with a server before running.

blocks.name: Crysis
blocks.text: Built for hardware that did not exist yet, on the assumption that clock speeds would keep climbing. They did not, and can it run Crysis became a benchmark question for the next decade because nothing could run it well for years.

blocks.name: Grand Theft Auto V (PC)
blocks.text: The install is larger than the entire hard disk of a high end machine from 2001.

blocks.name: Call of Duty: Modern Warfare
blocks.text: Large enough that internet providers noticed the update traffic, and large enough that a single game could fill the SSD in a typical laptop.

blocks.name: Typical major release
blocks.spec: 100 to 150 GB, 16 GB RAM, SSD required
blocks.text: Requiring an SSD rather than recommending one is new. Games now stream assets from storage while you play instead of loading everything up front, so a mechanical drive is not slow, it is unusable.

blocks.title: The web, which nobody designed to be this heavy
blocks.text: No single decision made web pages large. Each addition was individually reasonable: images, then better images, then fonts, then analytics, then video, then frameworks that make development faster at the cost of code the visitor has to download. The result is that an average page today transfers more data than the entire Windows 95 installer.

blocks.name: An average web page
blocks.text: A page was text and perhaps one image, because most people were connected at 28,800 bits per second and anything larger simply would not arrive.

blocks.name: An average web page
blocks.text: Broadband arrives and the constraint relaxes. Pages get images.

blocks.name: An average web page
blocks.text: Larger images, embedded video, social buttons, tracking scripts.

blocks.name: An average web page
blocks.spec: ~2.7 MB, over half of it images and scripts
blocks.text: Roughly two hundred times the 1995 figure, for pages that mostly show the same thing: some text and a picture. This is the clearest example on the page of capability being consumed rather than banked.

blocks.title: Capability against demand
blocks.text: Hardware and the software that ran on it, on one scale. The lines rise together, which is the point. When a hardware line flattens, look at whether the software line above it flattens too.

blocks.alt: Hardware capability against software requirements from 1981 to 2025
blocks.caption: All values in megabytes. Memory fitted and OS requirement are directly comparable; game install size and web page size are shown on the same scale to compare their shape.

blocks.title: Was any of it wasted?
blocks.text: The uncharitable reading is that developers stopped caring because hardware would cover for them. The charitable reading is that a 1995 machine could not have shown you a video call, encrypted your connection, rendered a font smoothly at any size or protected one program from another, and all of that costs something. Both readings are partly right, and working out which applies to a particular piece of software is a more interesting question than the general complaint.
